structure.title: I. The Duke Endowment and Hospital Care in North Carolina
IV. Results (A-C: hospitals, physicians, infant mortality)

observations.statement: Paper states its main empirical approach is a difference-in-differences design with staggered treatment adoption, comparing counties that received a Duke funding commitment to counties without one, and cohorts born before versus after that commitment.
observations.quote: a difference-in-differences design that exploits quasi-random variation in Duke support

observations.statement: Preferred model is described as an extensive-margin intent-to-treat specification, justified because Duke treatment involved multiple non-monetary requirements rather than a single payment, so treatment turns on at the first appropriation year.
Paper explicitly names differential pre-trends and selection into treatment as the two primary threats to identification and previews that neither is found to drive the results.

Methods section names the alternative staggered-adoption estimators used to check the two-way fixed effects design: stacked regression, extended two-way fixed effects, and the Callaway and Sant'Anna group-time estimator.

Data section lists several hand-collected and archival sources combined into a county-by-year-of-birth panel: Duke Endowment annual reports, AMA hospital service records, the American Medical Directory, North Carolina death certificates, and birth registers.

Main infant-mortality panel covers 1922 to 1942; the start year is set by the earliest availability of births by race and the end year is chosen to precede most post-1942 funding rollout and to avoid World War II era confounds.
Analysis is restricted to North Carolina alone, even though the Duke Endowment also operated in South Carolina, because comparable birth and mortality data are not available for South Carolina.

Long-run mortality sample uses restricted public-use Social Security Numident records and is limited to birth cohorts and follow-up ages chosen so every cohort is observed the same number of times, avoiding survival bias from incomplete pre-1988 coverage.

Paper distinguishes appropriations (funding commitments) from actual payments throughout, noting that not all appropriations converted into payments and using this distinction to define the intensive-margin treatment measures.

Treatment is an indicator equal to one starting the calendar year a county first received a Duke Endowment capital appropriation and remaining one thereafter, an extensive-margin intent-to-treat measure rather than a dollar amount.

Infant mortality rate is built by aggregating individual death certificates to county-by-year-of-birth cells and dividing by births from a separate vital-statistics series; both death counts and mortality rates are used as alternative dependent variables.

For an intensive-margin robustness check, the paper builds an instrument interacting a time-varying source of Endowment income growth with a cross-sectional indicator for whether a county already had a not-for-profit hospital when the Endowment was founded.

Physician quality is defined categorically, using whether a doctor's medical school required a two-year pre-admission degree well before the physician's own graduation, following a classification adapted from prior literature rather than a continuous index.

Paper discusses that vital-statistics death reporting switched from place of occurrence to place of residence partway through the sample period and explains how this reporting change constrains which years and geographies can be used.

Main hospital, physician, and infant-mortality tables follow the same column progression: an unweighted baseline, then a version adding weights, then a version adding both weights and the control-variable vector, so the marginal effect of each addition is visible.
Every main results table reports observation counts for each column and panel, including separately for the pooled, Black-only, and White-only subsamples.

Table notes state which fixed effects are included, whether weights and controls are used, and that standard errors are clustered at the county level, repeating this information at the bottom of every main table.
Notes specify that weighted columns weight observations by the number of births in a county-year or county-AMD-wave, distinguishing them from unweighted columns in the same table.

Rather than printing the dependent-variable mean inside each main table, the paper computes percentage effects at the sample mean in the running text and points readers to a separate summary-statistics table placed in the online appendix.
All main and robustness specifications cluster standard errors at the county level, justified in the methods section as accounting for correlated errors within a county.

Paper implements a randomization-inference exercise that reassigns the observed treatment paths of the treated counties (48 counties) to random subsets of North Carolina counties, using the resulting placebo distribution to build a second, design-based significance check.

For the instrumental-variables robustness check, the paper reports Anderson-Rubin confidence sets and tF confidence intervals rather than relying on a conventional first-stage F-statistic alone, stating this is meant to show instrument strength is not a concern.

Beyond stating that county-clustered standard errors capture within-county correlation, the paper does not explain why it computes Poisson-model standard errors via the delta method specifically, rather than an alternative such as a bootstrap.

Paper reports a covariate-balance test following an existing published approach for evaluating whether pretreatment changes in covariates predict treatment, placing the balance table in the online appendix and summarizing the joint test result in the main text.

Event-study figures for hospitals, physicians, and infant mortality are placed in the main text as the primary way of checking pre-trends, with the discussion explicitly describing the absence of significant pre-period coefficients as support for the identifying assumption.

Separately from randomization inference, the paper runs a placebo check that assigns fake treatment to non-Carolina Southern counties chosen to resemble the true treated counties, reporting that estimated placebo effects are small and inconsistently signed.

A footnote reports a fertility and maternal-mortality check meant to rule out that the number of births used both as the mortality-rate denominator and as regression weights is itself confounded by treatment.

Paper reports a Goodman-Bacon decomposition of the two-way fixed effects estimator in the online appendix and summarizes in the main text that comparisons between treated and never-treated counties receive most of the estimation weight.

Robustness to alternative staggered-adoption estimators (stacked regression, extended two-way fixed effects, Callaway and Sant'Anna) is summarized visually inside the main-text event-study figures rather than in a separate robustness table for each estimator.

Paper reports several alternative control-group constructions as robustness checks: adding non-Carolina Southern counties, restricting to propensity-score-matched Southern counties, and versions that also drop untreated North Carolina counties.

A single figure summarizes many sample and specification variants together, such as changing the panel's start and end years, dropping small counties, and altering how stillbirths and unnamed infant deaths are handled, as point estimates on one shared axis.

Paper reports robustness to expressing the dependent variable as a death count, a rate, or a log-transformed rate, treating these as alternative functional-form choices rather than committing to one form throughout.

Long-run mortality robustness checks (collapsing to cohort-level cumulative mortality, adding non-Carolina controls, adding South Carolina to the treatment group) are each pointed to a single named online-appendix table rather than reproduced in the main text.

Effects are reported separately by infant race (Black versus White) as a core part of every main results table, framed already in the introduction and design discussion as a primary object of interest rather than an exploratory cut added later.

Paper reports a formal test of whether the Black and White treatment-effect coefficients differ, taken from a model that fully interacts all right-hand-side variables with race and presented in a dedicated row beneath the race-specific panels of each table.

First-stage results on hospital beds, hospital counts, and physician counts and quality are presented as the mechanism through which Duke funding is argued to affect mortality, and are ordered to precede the mortality results in the paper.

Interaction between Duke support and the arrival of sulfa drugs is tested with a shift-share-style specification, interpreted as evidence that hospital modernization and medical innovation act as complements rather than substitutes.

Infant-mortality effect sizes are benchmarked against estimates from other historical US health interventions, including the Sheppard-Towner Act, midwifery licensing reforms, and Medicaid-introduction studies, to argue the magnitudes are plausible relative to that literature.

Paper converts its coefficient on hospital beds into a change evaluated at the sample mean, and separately computes what share of the overall historical decline in infant mortality could be attributed to Duke support using a back-of-envelope calculation.

A cost-effectiveness calculation divides total Duke expenditure by the estimated number of infant lives saved and compares the resulting per-life cost against value-of-statistical-life estimates from the literature to argue the program was cost-effective.

Conclusion cautions that a similar hospital-modernization intervention today would likely have a smaller effect at higher cost, because baseline health and health-care access are now much higher than during the study period.

Paper acknowledges that its focus on infant mortality is shaped partly by data availability and that it cannot observe other outcomes, such as human capital or wages, that plausibly also improved for the treated cohorts.

Discussion links the Duke Endowment program to the later Hill-Burton Act and argues the historical intervention may generalize to modern under-resourced settings, including rural regions of less-developed countries, while noting the extrapolation is speculative.

Each event-study figure layers three panel types together: raw treatment-versus-control trends over calendar time, trends normalized to the year before treatment, and event-study coefficient plots with confidence intervals, repeated across several outcome subgroups.

Figure 1 combines a rollout-share time series, a county-level map of first-funding timing, a raw mortality-by-race time series, and a map of county-level mortality change into one four-panel descriptive figure that precedes the methods section.

Main results tables report coefficients with standard errors in parentheses but do not mark significance with stars, leaving readers to judge precision from the reported standard errors, confidence intervals, or discussed p-values in the text.

Table notes specify which observations are dropped in race-split panels (counties with zero race-specific births in some year), letting readers see how the race-specific sample differs from the pooled sample without consulting the main text.

Introduction previews the paper's first-stage and mortality findings and closes with a sequence of numbered contribution paragraphs situating the study relative to several literatures before moving into the empirical sections.

Full data section, describing every source and variable, is placed before the methods section that lays out the regression equations, so the design is introduced only after each variable's construction has already been explained.

A dedicated robustness section follows the long-run mortality results and precedes the conclusion, and it leans heavily on named online-appendix tables and figures for the details of each check rather than reproducing them in the main text.

The medical-innovation interaction analysis, framed by the paper as mechanism evidence, is placed after the core infant-mortality results and before the long-run mortality section, rather than preceding the main results.

Reference list cites a replication data package for the paper deposited with the Inter-university Consortium for Political and Social Research under the American Economic Association's publisher listing, identified by its own DOI separate from the article DOI.

A first-page footnote directs readers to the article's online page for additional materials and author disclosure statements, rather than describing data-use or access procedures within the paper's own text.

Long-run mortality analysis is explicitly described as using the restricted, public-use version of Social Security Numident records obtained through the National Archives, distinguishing this from the openly available vital-statistics and directory sources used elsewhere.

gaps: No preregistration, pre-analysis plan, or IRB/ethics statement found anywhere in the main text.
No explicit multiple-testing adjustment stated despite reporting many outcome subgroups (race splits) and robustness variants.
No dedicated summary-statistics table appears in the main text itself; it is referenced as being in the online appendix (Tables N1-N2), which is not part of the provided text.
No explicit statement of statistical software beyond what can be inferred from the recipe card's Stata commands (reghdfe, csdid); the main text does not name software packages directly.
No formal density or manipulation test is reported, consistent with the design not relying on a running-variable cutoff.

reading.note: Read the entire 38-page article text in full, including introduction, historical background, data, methods, first-stage results, infant-mortality results, sulfa-drug interaction, long-run mortality, robustness checks, conclusion, and the reference list. The provided PDF/text does not include the paper's online appendix, which is cited repeatedly but was not available to read.
